text.en: Raju read about knights in armour. "Were there really knights?" he asked.

The term Middle Ages often describes a period in Europe after western Roman imperial rule. This chapter also follows societies in China, Japan, the Islamic world and the Ottoman Empire. In some parts of medieval Europe, landholding was linked to duties and loyalty. Lords, vassals, knights and peasants had different roles. Arrangements varied across places and centuries. Church institutions held religious, educational and economic influence across much of medieval western Europe.
The Crusades were several campaigns connected with religion, political power and territory. Jerusalem was a major focus of some campaigns. Trade and towns grew again, and guilds of merchants and craftsmen formed. Islam began in Arabia and spread over time. The regions ruled by Muslim dynasties became home to many communities and centres of scholarship.
The fourteenth-century Black Death caused severe population losses in Europe and elsewhere. Its effects on work and landholding differed by place. New universities, such as Bologna and Oxford, appeared.

text.en: The term Middle Ages is a historical period label. Textbooks use it to make comparisons across several centuries. Its dates and turning points do not fit every region equally.

board.text: Period labels depend on region and question

text.en: Tang rulers governed China through a central administration and regional officials. The capital at Chang’an became a centre of trade, learning and exchange.

board.text: Tang: administration, trade and an important capital

text.en: Examinations offered one route into official service in imperial China. Family resources and status still influenced who could prepare for and obtain positions.

board.text: Examinations were one route into government

text.en: During the Song period, towns, markets and production expanded in parts of China. Printing helped texts circulate and supports evidence about learning and government.

board.text: Song period: expanding markets and circulation of texts

text.en: The Mongols established the Yuan dynasty in China under Kublai Khan. The Ming dynasty came later. Place the names in order before comparing their institutions.

board.text: Tang → Song → Yuan → Ming, with transitions in between

text.en: Japan had an imperial court, but shoguns later held great military and political power. Imperial authority and military authority could coexist in different forms.

board.text: Imperial court and shogunate had different roles

text.en: Samurai belonged to a warrior class. Their relationships with lords changed over time. Compare these relationships with European examples without treating the systems as identical.

board.text: Comparison does not make two institutions identical

text.en: Islam originated in Arabia in the seventh century. The chapter links its early development with the Prophet Muhammad and the communities that followed his teachings.

board.text: Origin of Islam: seventh-century Arabia

text.en: A caliph was a leader in early Islamic political history. The Umayyad and Abbasid dynasties ruled at different times and used different centres of power.

board.text: Umayyad and Abbasid were distinct dynasties

text.en: Baghdad became a major Abbasid centre. Scholars worked with texts and ideas from different languages and regions. Translation could preserve, compare and extend earlier knowledge.

board.text: Baghdad: scholarship and translation

text.en: Merchants and travellers connected cities across land and sea. Exchange could move goods, languages and ideas without making everyone’s religion or customs the same.

board.text: Trade links communities with different practices

text.en: The Ottoman state grew from a base in Anatolia. Over time it governed territories across parts of Europe, Asia and Africa.

board.text: Ottoman growth began in Anatolia

text.en: The Ottomans captured Constantinople in 1453. This ended the Byzantine Empire and changed control of an important city between major trade routes.

board.text: 1453: conquest of Constantinople

text.en: Many European lords held land and received obligations from people who used it. Vassalage can describe a relationship of loyalty and service among people with power.

board.text: Vassalage relates to loyalty and service

text.en: A manor could include a lord’s land, peasant holdings and shared resources. Peasants did much of the farming. Their rents, labour obligations and ability to move varied.

board.text: Manor: place and organisation of rural work

text.en: Serfs were peasants whose freedom was restricted by customary obligations. Some peasants were free. Read a rule about one manor before drawing a conclusion about a whole region.

board.text: Peasants did not all have the same legal status

text.en: Monasteries and churches performed varied roles. Some kept records, educated people or provided assistance. Church institutions could also hold land.

board.text: Church institutions had several social roles

text.en: The Crusades involved military campaigns and wider connections among rulers and communities. Jerusalem mattered to several faiths. The campaigns differed in purpose and outcome.

board.text: Avoid reducing all campaigns to one event

text.en: Towns could offer markets for rural produce and workshops for craft goods. Guilds could set rules for a trade and organise training or membership.

board.text: Guilds organised some urban trades

text.en: Medieval universities developed as communities of teachers and learners. Bologna and Oxford are examples. Schools, courts and monasteries also supported learning.

board.text: Universities were one form of medieval learning

text.en: The Black Death disrupted families, settlements and work. In some places a shortage of workers changed bargaining over pay or obligations. Such effects varied across regions.

board.text: Population losses could affect work and obligations

text.en: To compare two societies, choose the same question in each. Ask who governed, who paid duties and which sources preserve their voices. Similar answers need supporting evidence.

board.text: Compare authority, duties and sources

problem.en: How can a village rent record and a guild rule show different kinds of medieval organisation?

text.en: Read the village record for obligations concerning land.

why.en: It may show rent or labour owed by a household.

text.en: Read the guild rule for obligations concerning a trade.

why.en: It may show how an urban occupation organised training or membership.

requiredIdeas.en: Serfs worked the land for lords.

points.en: Feudalism was a system of land and loyalty.
Church institutions held varied roles in medieval western Europe.
Jerusalem was a major focus of some Crusades.
